blocks.p: Then he ordered the word to be given out, and the word at that time was “Emmanuel.” Then the alarm was sounded, the battering-rams were set to work, and the slings whirled stones into the town with all their force; and so the battle began. Now Diabolus himself directed the townsmen at every gate, which made their resistance all the fiercer, more hellish, and more offensive to Emmanuel. So for several days the good Prince was held off by Diabolus and Mansoul; and it was a sight worth seeing, how the captains of Shaddai carried themselves in this war.

First, Captain Boanerges (not to undervalue the rest) made three furious assaults, one after another, on Ear-gate, until its posts shook. Captain Conviction closed up with Boanerges as fast as he possibly could, and when both saw that the gate was beginning to give, they ordered the rams to be kept at work against it. Now Captain Conviction, going up very near the gate, was driven back with great force and received three wounds in the mouth. And those who rode as volunteers went about encouraging the captains.

For the valor of these two captains, the Prince sent for them to his pavilion and ordered them to rest a while and be given something to refresh them. Care was also taken that Captain Conviction’s wounds should be healed. The Prince also gave each of them a chain of gold, and told them to keep up their courage.

Nor did Captain Good-Hope or Captain Charity lag behind in this desperate fight, for they did so well at Eye-gate that they had almost broken it wide open. They too had a reward from their Prince, as did the rest of the captains, because they fought valiantly all around the town.

In this engagement several of Diabolus’s officers were killed, and some of the townsmen wounded. Among the officers, one Captain Boasting was killed. This Boasting had thought that nobody could shake the posts of Ear-gate, or shake the heart of Diabolus. Next to him, one Captain Secure was killed. This Secure used to say that the blind and the lame in Mansoul could hold the gates of the town against Emmanuel’s army. It was Captain Conviction who split Captain Secure’s head with a two-handed sword, at the same time that he himself received the three wounds in his mouth.

Besides these there was one Captain Bragman, a thoroughly desperate fellow, who commanded a band of those who threw firebrands, arrows, and death; and he too received a mortal wound in the chest, from the hand of Captain Good-Hope at Eye-gate.

There was also one Mr. Feeling. He was no captain, but he was a great agitator, always stirring Mansoul up to rebellion. He received a wound in the eye from one of Boanerges’ soldiers, and would have been killed by the captain himself if he had not made a sudden retreat.

But I never saw Willbewill so daunted in all my life. He could not do what he used to do; and some say that he also took a wound in the leg, and that some of the men in the Prince’s army certainly saw him limping as he walked on the wall afterward.

I will not list the names of the soldiers killed in the town, for many were maimed, wounded, and killed. When they saw the posts of Ear-gate shaking, and Eye-gate nearly broken open, and their captains dead, it took the heart out of many of the Diabolonians; and they fell also under the shot that the golden slings sent into the very middle of Mansoul.
Among the townsmen there was one Love-no-Good. He was a townsman, but a Diabolonian; he too received his mortal wound in Mansoul, though he did not die very soon.

Mr. Dwell-on-it also, the one who had come along with Diabolus when he first set out to take Mansoul, received a terrible wound in the head; some say his skull was cracked. This I have noticed: he was never again able to do Mansoul the kind of harm he had done in times past. Old Prejudice and Mr. Any-side fled as well.

Now when the battle was over, the Prince ordered that the white flag should be set up once more on Mount Gracious, in sight of the town of Mansoul, to show that Emmanuel still had grace for the wretched town of Mansoul.

When Diabolus saw the white flag hung out again, knowing that it was not for him but for Mansoul, he decided to play another trick: to see whether Emmanuel would raise his siege and be gone on a promise of reform. So one evening, a good while after sunset, he came down to the gate and called to speak with Emmanuel, who came down at once; and Diabolus said to him:
“Since you make it plain by your white flag that you are wholly given to peace and quiet, I thought it right to let you know that we are ready to accept it, on terms you may agree to.

“I know that you are devoted to godliness, and that holiness pleases you; yes, that your great aim in making war on Mansoul is that it may be a holy dwelling place. Well then, draw your forces off from the town, and I will bend Mansoul to your bow.

“First, I will lay down all acts of hostility against you, and I will be willing to become your deputy; and as I have been against you before, so now I will serve you in the town of Mansoul. And to be more particular:
“One, I will persuade Mansoul to receive you as their Lord; and I know they will do it all the sooner when they understand that I am your deputy.
“Two, I will show them where they have gone wrong, and that transgression stands in the way of life.
“Three, I will show them the holy law they must conform to, the very law they have broken.
“Four, I will press on them the necessity of reforming according to your law.
“Five, so that none of these things may fail, I myself, at my own cost and expense, will set up and maintain a sufficient ministry in Mansoul, and lectures besides.
“Six, you shall receive from us, year by year, whatever you think fit to lay and levy on us, as a token of our subjection to you.”

Then Emmanuel said to him, “You who are full of deceit, how shifting your ways are! How often you have changed and changed again, if only you might keep possession of my Mansoul, though, as has been plainly declared before, I am its rightful heir! You have made your proposals often enough already, and this last is not a bit better than the rest. And having failed to deceive when you showed yourself in your black, you have now transformed yourself into an angel of light, and would pass for a minister of righteousness, the better to deceive.

“But know this, Diabolus: nothing you can propose is to be regarded, for you do nothing except to deceive. You have neither conscience toward God nor love for the town of Mansoul; so where can these words of yours come from, but from sinful craft and deceit? Anyone who will propose whatever he pleases, at his own whim, and use it to destroy those who believe him, must be abandoned, along with everything he says. But if righteousness is such a beauty in your eyes now, how is it that you clung so closely to wickedness before? But that is by the way.

“You talk now of reform in Mansoul, and say that you yourself, if I please, will be at the head of that reform; all the while knowing that the greatest progress a man can make in the law and its righteousness will do nothing at all, nothing, toward taking the curse away from Mansoul. For when a law has been broken by Mansoul, a law that already carried God’s curse against anyone who should break it, he can never free himself from that curse by obeying the law afterward (to say nothing of what kind of reform is likely to be set up in Mansoul when the devil has become the corrector of vice). You know that everything you have said in this matter is nothing but guile and deceit; and as it was your first card, so it is the last card you have to play. Many quickly see through you when you show them your cloven foot; but in your white, in your light, in your disguise, you are seen for what you are by only a few. But you shall not deal like this with my Mansoul, Diabolus; for I still love my Mansoul.

“Besides, I have not come to set Mansoul to living by its works. If I did that, I would be like you. I have come so that through me, and through what I have done and will do for Mansoul, they may be reconciled to my Father, though by their sin they have provoked him to anger, and though by the law they cannot obtain mercy.

“You talk of bringing this town under what is good, when nobody wants it from your hands. I am sent by my Father to possess it myself, and to guide it by the skill of my own hands into such likeness to him as will be pleasing in his sight. So I will possess it myself. I will dispossess you and cast you out. I will set up my own standard in the middle of them. I will govern them by new laws, new officers, new motives, and new ways. Yes, I will pull this town down and build it again; and it shall be as though it had never been, and then it shall be the glory of the whole universe.”

When Diabolus heard this, and saw that all his deceits were found out, he was confounded and completely at a loss. But having in himself the fountain of wickedness, rage, and malice against Shaddai and his Son and the beloved town of Mansoul, what did he do but strengthen himself as best he could to give fresh battle to the noble Prince Emmanuel? So now we must have another fight before the town of Mansoul is taken. Come up to the mountains, then, you who love to watch military action, and see on both sides how the fatal blow is struck, while one seeks to hold the famous town of Mansoul and the other seeks to make himself its master.

So Diabolus withdrew from the wall to his forces in the heart of the town of Mansoul, and Emmanuel returned to the camp; and each, in his own way, put himself into position to give battle to the other.

Diabolus, despairing of keeping the famous town of Mansoul in his hands, resolved to do all the harm he could (if indeed he could do any) to the Prince’s army and to the town. For, alas, it was never the happiness of foolish Mansoul that Diabolus had in mind, but its utter ruin and overthrow, as is plain enough now. So he ordered his officers that when they saw they could hold the town no longer, they should do it all the harm they could, rending and tearing men, women, and children. “For,” he said, “we had better demolish the place entirely and leave it a heap of ruins than leave it fit to be a dwelling for Emmanuel.”

Emmanuel, on his side, knowing that the next battle would make him master of the place, issued a royal command to all his officers, high captains, and men of war, to be sure to show themselves men of war against Diabolus and all the Diabolonians, but kind, merciful, and gentle toward the old inhabitants of Mansoul. “Turn the hottest front of the battle, then,” said the noble Prince, “against Diabolus and his men.”

So when the day came, the command was given, and the Prince’s men stood bravely to their arms and, as before, turned their main force against Ear-gate and Eye-gate. The word this time was “Mansoul is won!” and so they made their assault on the town. Diabolus, for his part, resisted from within as hard as he could with the bulk of his power, and for a time his high lords and chief captains fought very cruelly against the Prince’s army.

But after three or four notable charges by the Prince and his noble captains, Ear-gate was broken open, and the bars and bolts that had kept it shut against the Prince were smashed into a thousand pieces. Then the Prince’s trumpets sounded, the captains shouted, the town shook, and Diabolus retreated to his stronghold. When the Prince’s forces had broken open the gate, he himself came up and set his throne in it; and he set his standard beside it, on a mound his men had earlier thrown up to mount the mighty slings on. The mound was called Mount Hear-well. There the Prince stayed, close by the way in at the gate. He also ordered that the golden slings should still be played on the town, especially against the castle, because Diabolus had retreated there for shelter.

Now from Ear-gate the street ran straight to the house of Mr. Recorder, as he had been before Diabolus took the town; and close by his house stood the castle that Diabolus had long made his loathsome den. The captains quickly cleared that street with their slings, so that a way was opened to the heart of the town. Then the Prince ordered Captain Boanerges, Captain Conviction, and Captain Judgment to march at once up through the town to the old gentleman’s gate. So the captains entered the town of Mansoul in the most warlike manner, and marching in with flying colors, they came up to the Recorder’s house, which was almost as strong as the castle. They also brought battering-rams with them, to set against the castle gates.

When they came to the house of Mr. Conscience, they knocked and demanded entrance. Now the old gentleman, not yet fully knowing their purpose, had kept his gates shut all through this fight. So Boanerges demanded entrance at his gates; and when no one answered, he gave the gate one stroke with the head of a ram, which made the old gentleman shake and his house tremble and totter. Then Mr. Recorder came down to the gates and, as well as he could with quivering lips, asked who was there.

“We are the captains and commanders of the great Shaddai and of the blessed Emmanuel, his Son,” Boanerges answered, “and we demand possession of your house for the use of our noble Prince.” And with that the battering-ram gave the gate another shake.

This made the old gentleman tremble all the more; yet he did not dare do anything but open the gate. Then the King’s forces marched in, that is, the three brave captains I have named. Now the Recorder’s house suited Emmanuel well, not only because it was strong and near the castle, but because it was large and faced the castle, the den where Diabolus now hid, afraid to come out. As for Mr. Recorder, the captains were very reserved toward him. He still knew nothing of Emmanuel’s great designs, so he did not know what to make of things, or what would be the end of such thundering beginnings.

It was soon noised about the town that the Recorder’s house had been seized, his rooms taken over, and his palace made the seat of the war. No sooner was the news out than his friends took fright and passed it on to others; and you know how a snowball loses nothing by rolling. In a little while the whole town was convinced that they must expect nothing from the Prince but destruction. And the ground of the whole business was this: the Recorder was afraid, the Recorder trembled, and the captains behaved strangely toward the Recorder. So many came to see; but when they saw with their own eyes the captains in the palace, and their battering-rams forever pounding at the castle gates, they were fixed fast in their fears and left in a daze. And, as I said, the man of the house only added to it all; for whoever came to him, he would talk of nothing, tell nothing, and hear nothing, except that death and destruction now awaited Mansoul.

“For,” said the old gentleman, “you all know that we have been traitors to that once despised, but now famously victorious and glorious Prince Emmanuel. For now, as you see, he not only lies in close siege around us, but has forced his way in at our gates. What is more, Diabolus flees before him; and he has, as you see, made my house a garrison against the castle where Diabolus is. For my part, I have sinned greatly; it is well for the man who is clean. But I say I have sinned greatly, in keeping silent when I should have spoken, and in perverting justice when I should have carried it out. True, I suffered something at the hands of Diabolus for taking the side of King Shaddai’s laws; but alas, what good will that do? Will that make up for the rebellions and treasons I have committed, and have let be committed in the town of Mansoul without a word against them? Oh, I tremble to think what the end of so dreadful and so wrathful a beginning will be!”

Now while these brave captains were busy like this in the old Recorder’s house, Captain Execution was just as busy in other parts of the town, securing the back streets and the walls. He also hunted the Lord Willbewill hard. He gave him no rest in any corner; he pursued him so closely that he drove his men away from him and made him glad to thrust his head into a hole. This mighty warrior also cut down three of the Lord Willbewill’s officers. One was old Mr. Prejudice, the one who had his head cracked in the mutiny. Lord Willbewill had made this man keeper of Ear-gate, and he fell by the hand of Captain Execution. Another of Lord Willbewill’s officers, one Mr. Backward-to-all-but-evil, captain of the two guns once mounted on top of Ear-gate, was also cut down by Captain Execution. The third was Captain Treacherous, a vile man, but one in whom Willbewill put a great deal of confidence; and Captain Execution cut him down with the rest.

He also made a very great slaughter among my Lord Willbewill’s soldiers, killing many who were stout and sturdy, and wounding many who were quick and active for Diabolus. But all these were Diabolonians; not one man who was a native of Mansoul was hurt.

Other feats of war were performed by the other captains as well. At Eye-gate, where Captain Good-Hope and Captain Charity were in command, great execution was done; for Captain Good-Hope with his own hands killed one Captain Blindfold, the keeper of that gate. This Blindfold was captain of a thousand men, and they were the ones who fought with mauls. Captain Good-Hope also pursued his men, killed many, wounded more, and made the rest hide their heads in corners.

Also at that gate was Mr. Dwell-on-it, whom you have heard of before. He was an old man with a beard that reached down to his belt, the same who had been orator to Diabolus. He had done much harm in the town of Mansoul, and now he fell by the hand of Captain Good-Hope.
What more shall I say? In those days the Diabolonians lay dead in every corner, though too many were still alive in Mansoul.
